Speculative decoding works by having a small, cheap draft model propose several tokens at once, which a larger target model then verifies in parallel — accepting a token only if its distribution sufficiently matches what the target would have chosen. The central question here is: when the input domain shifts (say, from general web text to clinical notes or legal contracts), how quickly and how severely does the draft model's proposal quality degrade, and does that degradation happen smoothly or in sudden drops? The key concepts to hold together are acceptance rate (the fraction of draft tokens the target accepts per forward pass), KL divergence between draft and target distributions at each position, and domain shift as a covariate that widens that divergence in ways that are not uniform across token positions or sequence lengths. A beginner assumes acceptance rate is roughly stable as long as the draft model is "pretty good" and the domain isn't wildly different — what an expert worries about is that divergence is highly heterogeneous: certain syntactic constructions or rare domain-specific tokens cause localized acceptance collapses that corrupt entire speculative windows, meaning the effective speedup can crater without any obvious warning signal in aggregate metrics. The deeper concern is that acceptance rate stability is often measured on held-out test sets from the same distribution used to train or select the draft model, so production domain shift is essentially invisible until latency degrades in deployment.

A naive evaluation metric — mean acceptance rate averaged across a held-out test set — masks exactly the failure mode that matters, because it lets a high acceptance rate on common tokens statistically swamp the catastrophic collapse on rare but semantically critical ones. In clinical text, for instance, drug names, dosage units, and lab value tokens might constitute 3-5% of the token stream but carry nearly all the semantic load; a draft model achieving 85% mean acceptance rate could be accepting virtually none of those tokens while looking healthy in aggregate. What this implies is that evaluation needs stratified acceptance rate measurement — broken out by token frequency bucket, part-of-speech or syntactic role, and domain-specific entity type — so that tail-token performance is visible. The Medusa paper (Cai et al., 2024) and follow-on work on SpecInfer implicitly acknowledge this by reporting acceptance rates on domain-specific benchmarks separately, but even those don't decompose by token category within the benchmark. A more rigorous approach would track acceptance rate conditioned on the target model's own confidence (its top-1 probability): when the target is uncertain — precisely the high-information, domain-specific positions — that's where draft divergence is most damaging and most invisible to mean metrics. The practical implication is that draft model selection for a new domain should include a worst-decile acceptance rate statistic, not just the mean, analogous to how financial risk modeling uses CVaR rather than expected loss.

The tradeoff is real and has a clean information-theoretic framing: speculative decoding gains efficiency precisely by exploiting regions where the draft and target agree, but target uncertainty and draft-target divergence are positively correlated under domain shift, so the regime where you most need the target's judgment is exactly the regime where speculative proposals are least trustworthy — you're paying verification cost for proposals you'll mostly reject. This isn't just theoretical; SpecTr (Sun et al., 2023) and the rejection sampling analysis in the original speculative decoding paper (Leviathan et al., 2023) both show acceptance rate dropping nonlinearly as draft-target KL increases, meaning efficiency degrades faster than divergence grows — a convexity that punishes domain shift disproportionately. The principled early-detection approach that has gotten the most traction is using the draft model's own uncertainty as a proxy signal: if the draft's entropy at position t exceeds a learned threshold, you truncate the speculative window early rather than proposing tokens the target will likely reject. This is essentially what adaptive speculative decoding schemes like SpecDec++ and Draft & Verify implement — dynamic window length conditioned on draft confidence — and they report recovering 10-20% of the acceptance rate loss from naive fixed-window speculation under distribution shift. A cleaner signal, though underexplored in production systems, is the draft model's rank of the target's previously accepted token: if the target has been consistently choosing tokens the draft ranked 3rd or 4th rather than 1st, that's a leading indicator of entering a high-divergence region before the current window fully plays out. The fundamental limitation is that all these signals are proxies — draft entropy is cheap but measures draft uncertainty, not draft-target disagreement specifically, and those diverge (ironically) most under domain shift.

Miscalibrated draft entropy fails in two distinct and opposite ways: an overconfident draft (entropy too low relative to true uncertainty) never triggers truncation when it should, so you burn verification budget on high-divergence windows and acceptance rate collapses silently; an underconfident draft (entropy too high everywhere) truncates aggressively even in easy regions, destroying the speedup even when the domain hasn't actually shifted. The overconfidence failure is more dangerous in practice because it's invisible — the system appears to be speculating normally while actually generating a high rejection rate, and the only observable symptom is increased mean latency, which operators often attribute to load rather than draft miscalibration. This is a concrete instance of the general LLM calibration problem documented by Guo et al. (2017) on temperature scaling: models trained with cross-entropy to maximize likelihood tend to be overconfident, and smaller draft models are often worse-calibrated than their larger counterparts because they've been distilled or pruned in ways that don't preserve the softmax temperature structure. Detecting that the entropy signal has gone wrong requires tracking the empirical correlation between draft entropy at position t and actual acceptance at position t across a rolling window of recent inferences — if high-entropy predictions are being accepted at the same rate as low-entropy ones, the entropy signal has lost its discriminative power as a truncation cue. The subtlety is that this correlation can degrade gradually under slow domain shift — a phenomenon analogous to covariate shift in supervised learning — so a threshold-based detector will lag the actual miscalibration by potentially thousands of inference steps. The cleanest fix would be online temperature recalibration of the draft model conditioned on recent acceptance outcomes, but no production speculative decoding system I'm aware of implements this; it remains an open engineering gap despite the theoretical machinery being well-understood from the calibration literature.

The feedback loop has the structure of a control system where the plant is draft temperature, the sensor is empirical acceptance rate, and the setpoint is some target acceptance rate — and like any such system, stability requires that the loop gain be bounded and the sensor signal not be corrupted by the very actuation you're applying. The critical instability mode is this: if you raise temperature in response to low acceptance rate (correct response to overconfidence), the wider draft distribution increases entropy, which causes more aggressive truncation, which means fewer tokens are proposed and verified, which reduces the sample size for your acceptance rate estimate — so your sensor degrades precisely when you're making the largest corrections, a classic gain-bandwidth tradeoff that leads to oscillation or runaway. Stability conditions in the control-theoretic sense require the learning rate on temperature updates to be smaller than the inverse of the acceptance rate variance, which itself depends on window length and domain difficulty — in practice this means slow-moving exponential moving averages (decay ~0.99 or slower) are far safer than aggressive online updates, at the cost of slow adaptation to genuine domain shift. The divergence scenario that's most dangerous isn't gradual domain shift but punctuated shift — a sudden change in input distribution (a user switching from English prose to code, or from narrative to tabular data mid-session) where the acceptance rate signal drops sharply, the temperature correction overshoots, truncation becomes so aggressive that window length collapses to 1, and the system effectively abandons speculative decoding entirely while the temperature controller keeps pushing. There's a direct analogy here to reward hacking in RL fine-tuning: the optimizer (temperature controller) finds a degenerate solution (always truncate at position 1) that satisfies the local signal (acceptance rate is now 100% because you never propose tokens that get rejected) while completely defeating the purpose of the mechanism. Avoiding this requires a floor constraint on mean window length as a second control variable — essentially a multi-objective controller — but this adds a hyperparameter that itself needs domain-specific tuning, which is precisely the problem you were trying to avoid by going online in the first place.

The key insight is that acceptance rate and window length are jointly sufficient to detect the collapse — acceptance rate alone is blind to it, but the product of mean accepted tokens per forward pass (effective throughput tokens) divided by mean forward passes per output token gives you a speedup proxy that doesn't require knowing the ground-truth ratio. In a healthy speculative decoding system, this product should be substantially greater than 1; when window length collapses to 1, it converges to exactly 1 regardless of acceptance rate, and that signature is unambiguous. A second independent observable is the distribution of window lengths actually proposed versus accepted: in normal operation you see a right-skewed distribution where many windows are fully accepted; in the degenerate state the distribution collapses to a spike at 1, which is detectable with a simple KS test against a reference window-length histogram collected during healthy operation. A third signal, underutilized in practice, is draft model forward pass wall-clock time as a fraction of total inference time — in healthy speculative decoding, draft passes are cheap and frequent relative to target passes; when speculation collapses, the ratio of draft-to-target compute invocations drops toward zero, which is measurable at the infrastructure layer without any knowledge of token content. The practical instrumentation recommendation is a dashboard tracking three time-series: mean proposed window length, mean accepted window length, and the draft-to-target forward-pass ratio — any of these trending toward their degenerate values (1, 1, and 0 respectively) while acceptance rate stays high is a definitive signature of controller collapse rather than genuine calibration success. Systems like NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM expose some of these counters already, but they're rarely wired into alerting pipelines specifically for this failure mode, which is an operational gap in most production deployments.

Order of operations matters significantly because the two variables are coupled in a way that makes simultaneous reset dangerous: if you widen the window while temperature is still extreme (pushed high by the overconfident-overconfidence spiral), you immediately flood the target with low-quality proposals across a long window, producing a burst of rejections that the acceptance rate sensor reads as a new crisis and potentially re-triggers the controller before it has stabilized. The correct trajectory is temperature-first, window-second, with a hold period between them — concretely, reset temperature to a safe prior (the value from offline calibration on a general domain, or simply T=1.0 as a neutral default), then observe acceptance rate for enough forward passes to get a low-variance estimate (roughly 1/p passes where p is target acceptance rate, so ~5-20 passes at typical acceptance rates of 0.6-0.8), and only then begin widening the window incrementally. This sequencing is directly analogous to PID controller reset windup mitigation: when an integrator has saturated, standard practice is to clamp the integrator state back to a neutral value before re-engaging the plant, precisely because the saturated state encodes a false history that will drive the system in the wrong direction when load changes. The window widening itself should be gradual — increasing by 1 token per N forward passes rather than jumping to the pre-collapse window length — because the acceptance rate estimate at small window lengths is not predictive of acceptance rate at large window lengths under a freshly reset temperature; the joint distribution needs to be re-explored. A subtlety that's easy to miss: if the collapse was triggered by genuine punctuated domain shift rather than controller instability, resetting temperature to the general-domain prior is wrong — you need a temperature appropriate for the new domain, which you don't yet know. This argues for a brief exploration phase post-reset where temperature is treated as uncertain and sampled from a posterior rather than point-estimated, essentially a bandit-style recovery that explores temperature values while the window is still narrow and the cost of bad proposals is low.

The cleanest way to make exploration cost fall on the system rather than the user is to decouple exploration from the critical path entirely: run a shadow draft process at candidate temperatures in parallel with the live inference, discarding the shadow proposals but using their acceptance outcomes against the target's actual continuations to update the temperature posterior — this costs additional compute but adds zero latency from the user's perspective, and is feasible on hardware where the draft model is small enough that a second instance fits in spare GPU capacity alongside the target. The latency penalty of on-path exploration can be bounded by constraining exploration to the prefix of each speculative window: propose the first 1-2 tokens at the exploratory temperature and the remainder at the current best-estimate temperature, so that early rejection (the most informative signal) is cheap and late-window exploration cost is avoided — this is essentially a truncated experiment design that concentrates information gain at low window positions where the marginal cost of rejection is smallest. A tighter bound comes from recognizing that temperature exploration only needs to distinguish between a small number of candidate values — in practice you're searching a 1D continuous space that can be adequately covered by 3-5 discrete candidates — so the Bayesian regret bound for a Gaussian process bandit over that space is O(sqrt(T log T)) in the number of inference steps T, meaning the cumulative exploration penalty is sublinear and the per-step cost shrinks as the posterior concentrates. The user-visible manifestation of on-path exploration is not latency but output quality variance: at suboptimal temperatures the accepted tokens may be subtly worse, which is a different and arguably more serious harm than slowness, and one that latency metrics don't capture at all. This suggests the right objective for bounding exploration harm isn't latency penalty but KL divergence between outputs at exploratory vs. optimal temperature, and exploration should be gated by a constraint that this KL stays below a threshold — which you can estimate cheaply from the draft model's own distribution without running the target. Systems like Waymo's or Google's serving infrastructure that run multiple model variants in shadow mode for A/B evaluation have the architectural machinery for shadow draft exploration already; the gap is wiring temperature as the experimental variable rather than model weights.
